..
Issued at 230 PM CDT Wed Aug 26 2026

Water vapor satellite imagery and upper air analysis show a sharp 
upper trough continuing eastward across the Great Lakes region, and 
a mid/upper ridge axis across the central and northern Rockies. At 
the surface, a weak ridge is settling in across western North 
Dakota, and light northwest winds are gradually becoming even 
lighter and more variable this afternoon. Overnight tonight into 
Thursday morning, light winds and clear skies in association with 
this surface ridge will support optimal radiational cooling which 
may lead to patchy shallow fog in some of the river valleys and 
other lower elevation areas. However, given the presence of this 
drier air mass, coverage will be limited. Lows tonight should 
generally bottom out in the upper 40s to low 50s. Increasing 
southerly/southeasterly winds and ample diurnal heating should 
quickly mix out any fog that develops Thursday morning. The primary 
mid/upper ridge axis will nose out over eastern Montana and western 
North Dakota by Thursday afternoon, and this will support
slightly warmer temperatures with afternoon highs raging from 
upper 70s to upper 80s. It's possible a few locations across 
southwest North Dakota surpass the 90-degree mark. Additionally,
the aforementioned increasing southerly winds ahead of a 
strengthening surface trough across central Montana along with 
20-25% RH across western North Dakota could present some modest 
fire weather concerns, but recent rainfall should quell this 
concern some. Increasing cloud cover, along with breezy 
conditions keeping the boundary layer somewhat mixed, should 
keep Thursday night lows slightly above average in the upper 50s
to low 60s.

Several CAMs and global models are supporting the idea of a band of 
elevated showers and storms sweeping from west to east across the 
state from early Friday morning through early Friday afternoon. This 
idea is generally supported as widespread lift, caused by an axis of 
mid-level WAA traversing across the state in addition to an incoming 
shortwave trough rounding the northern periphery of the mid/upper 
ridge axis (which should be centered just east of the Rockies by 
Friday morning), overspreads much of the forecast area. MUCAPE 
around 1000-1500 J/kg and effective shear around 40 knots could 
support some organized convection capable of small hail. One caveat 
to Friday morning/early Friday afternoon storm chances will be some 
modest CIN across the region. However, the aforementioned synoptic 
lift should be more than enough to overcome this. Later in the day, 
uncertainty about the evolution of the leftover elevated convection 
and the potential for additional afternoon/evening surface-based 
convection remains relatively high. Questions that remain are: how 
quickly will elevated showers and storms exit eastward, how much 
does the atmosphere destabilize in the wake of this activity, and 
how far east is the next shortwave trough by Friday evening? 
Currently, guidance suggests destabilization of the atmosphere 
Friday afternoon will be confined to mainly southern North Dakota 
with the warm front likely staying south of I-94. However, the 
shortwave trough axis looks to still be out over western/central 
Montana by Friday evening keeping much of the broad ascent just west 
of the forecast area. Still, a surface-based storm or two cannot be 
ruled out along or south of the warm front Friday afternoon and 
evening. These potential storms could be strong to severe before the 
loss of diurnal heating late Friday evening/Friday night. Generally 
speaking, highs Friday afternoon will be slightly above average with 
low to mid 90s across southwest ND and upper 70s to low 80s across 
northern and eastern ND.

Mid range guidance suggests the primary mid/upper ridge axis will 
stall out across the central plains keeping zonal flow aloft across 
the north-central CONUS. Embedded shortwave impulses traversing in 
this flow aloft will support periodic chances for showers and storms 
across the forecast area through much of this weekend. Global 
guidance continues to suggest that sufficient instability and shear 
will be in place Saturday (and perhaps Sunday?) to support strong or 
marginally severe storms. Broad and deep troughing across the 
western CONUS will place southwesterly flow aloft across the 
northern plains early next week. A parade of shortwave troughs 
embedded in this flow will continue supporting periodic shower and 
storm chances through the middle of next week. Also, temperatures 
are forecast to remain near average this weekend into early next 
week.
